questions.q: In one line, what is an Episodic Pivot?
choices: A forgotten stock re-priced by news
A leader gapping on news out of a base
A stock gapping up for the third time
A quiet drift along the 50-day
questions.answer: A forgotten stock re-priced by news
questions.why: A forgotten stock re-priced by news. Neglect matters because a stock that did not rally into the report has not priced the news in. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings. Kullamagi: unexpected good news on a neglected stock can start a multi-month move. We look at the six months before the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Neglect plus a named surprise. That is the whole idea.

wrong.A stock gapping up for the third time: A third gap is late. Bonde says the EP is most valuable at the beginning of a move.
wrong.A quiet drift along the 50-day: That is the rest before the news, not the pivot. The pivot is the gap day itself.
wrong.A leader gapping on news out of a base: That is a Power Earnings Gap. We call an EP a neglected stock and a PEG an established leader gapping out of a base.

questions.simple: An EP is a forgotten stock that jumps on big news. It works because the market had not priced that news in.

reasons: stable definition; two Tier 2 originators agree

questions.q: An Episodic Pivot needs a named catalyst; a big gap on no news is not one.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A named catalyst gives buyers a reason to hold the gap. Bonde: earnings, new products and raised guidance have a high probability of triggering multi-month rallies. A media mention or an analyst upgrade alone has a low probability of follow-through. Price and volume are half the setup. The episode is the other half.
questions.lesson_line: Name the news before you name the setup. No episode, no pivot.
questions.simple: True. Without a named reason for the jump, buyers have little cause to hold the gap, so there is no pivot.

reasons: rests on the card's catalyst line, a held decision (D-032)

questions.q: What does neglect look like on the chart before the news?
choices: Flat or down for months, no rally
A steady uptrend above the 20 EMA
Flat for two weeks, then a sharp rally
A new high every week into the report
questions.answer: Flat or down for months, no rally
questions.why: Flat or down for months, with no rally into the news. A stock that rallied into the report has already priced some of the news in. One that sat flat has not. Bonde: neglect shows as no big rally before earnings, a long sideways stretch or a down move. Kullamagi: the best EPs come after 3 to 6 months or more of sideways trading. The stock on this chart sat flat to down for six months before its gap.
questions.lesson_line: The best surprise lands on a stock nobody was watching.

wrong.A new high every week into the report: New highs every week is a rally into the report. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings.
wrong.Flat for two weeks, then a sharp rally: A rally into the report is the opposite of neglect. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings.
wrong.A steady uptrend above the 20 EMA: A stock already trending up has been noticed. Bonde wants one that has not rallied into earnings.

questions.simple: Neglect is a stock flat or down for months. It has not priced in the news, so the surprise can re-price it.

reasons: stable idea; two Tier 2 originators agree

questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. Look at the months before it.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: When you buy the opening-range break, the stop goes a few cents under the low of the ___ at the time of entry.
questions.answer: day
questions.why: Day. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day at the time of entry, not exactly on it. Kullamagi: the stop is always at the lows of the day. On a delayed entry it goes under the trigger day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.simple: On day one the stop goes a few cents under the day's low at the moment you buy, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, stop under the day's low)

questions.q: The gap is holding and the volume is there. Where is the day-one buy?
choices: Over the opening-range high, at market
On a dip back to the prior close
On a limit order a bit under the open
At the close, if the gap held all day
questions.answer: Over the opening-range high, at market
questions.why: Over the opening-range high, at market, in regular hours. We buy as price trades through the trigger, never at the close. The opening range is the first 30 minutes of the day. Waiting for it is our default, but a strong move that triggers properly can be bought earlier. Buying over the range high keeps the low of the day close, so the stop stays tight and the full size fits. At the close the low can be 7% or more away. Kullamagi enters opening range highs with the stop at the lows of the day, and our GRRR note puts the stop at the low of the day too.
questions.lesson_line: The opening range is the trigger. The low of the day is the stop.

wrong.On a limit order a bit under the open: Our entries are market orders. A limit under the open can sit unfilled while the stock runs away.
wrong.At the close, if the gap held all day: We do not buy the close. By then the low of the day can be 7% or more under the price, past the 5% we accept, so we wait for a tighter trigger instead.
wrong.On a dip back to the prior close: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap and ends the setup, so there is nothing left to buy.

questions.simple: Buy at market when price trades over the opening-range high. The stop under the day's low stays close, so the size stays full.

reasons: rests on the day-one trigger, a held decision (D-005)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)

questions.q: Bonde made his biggest EP money buying pre-market, and that is how we buy them too.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Bonde did make his biggest EP money buying pre-market, and we do not. We make no new buys outside regular trading hours. Our buy needs a trigger and a stop. The opening-range high and the day's low only exist once the market is open. Kullamagi also rarely trades extended hours and waits for the opening-range high.
questions.lesson_line: Bonde's best buys were pre-market. Ours are not. Wait for the bell.
questions.simple: False. We buy in regular hours only, because the trigger and the stop come from the day's own range.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E58, regular hours)

questions.q: Which catalyst do we look at first when hunting an EP?
choices: An earnings report
An FDA decision
A sector move
An analyst upgrade
questions.answer: An earnings report
questions.why: An earnings report. It is dated, public and measurable, so you can check the growth and the beat before you buy. Bonde: earnings EPs are the easiest to understand and act on. Kullamagi had most success with earnings EPs. A big earnings gap alone is still not an EP. The stock needs neglect too, because Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied into earnings.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings first. The report is dated, public and measurable.

wrong.An FDA decision: Kullamagi says biotech EPs are the most difficult, so they are not the first place to look.
wrong.A sector move: Bonde lists sector moves as a high-probability catalyst, but he calls the earnings EP the easiest to act on.
wrong.An analyst upgrade: An analyst upgrade alone is on Bonde's low-probability list, so it is the last place to look.

questions.simple: Start with earnings, because the report is dated and public and you can check the numbers before you buy.

reasons: two Tier 2 originators agree on a stable point

questions.q: What is this, and what do you do?
choices: Not an EP; no long on this one
An EP; buy the first bounce
An EP; buy the close if it is green
A short; it will fill the gap
questions.story: A stock gaps up 11% on a report. By 10:30 it trades under its open on heavy volume.
questions.answer: Not an EP; no long on this one
questions.why: Not an EP, so there is no long here. A gap that sells off below the open means sellers are using the news to get out. Kullamagi says a stock that gapped up but sold off is not an EP. Heavy volume does not change that, because it is heavy on both sides. The gap must hold and close strong.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that cannot hold its open has told you everything. Walk away.

wrong.An EP; buy the first bounce: There is no trigger under the open. The buy needs the gap to hold and price above the opening-range high.
wrong.A short; it will fill the gap: Treating a gap as one that must fill is a named mistake. Not an EP means no long here, and nothing in the story gives a short.
wrong.An EP; buy the close if it is green: Green is not enough. It traded under the open, and a gap that sells off is not an EP.

questions.simple: It is not an EP. A gap that sells off under its open shows the sellers beating the buyers.

reasons: card line plus Kullamagi's own example

questions.q: A gap day that closes in the lower half of its range still counts as an EP if the volume was huge.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The gap day must close in the upper half of its range and never trade back to the prior close. Volume grades the day, but the close is a gate. We want bull gaps to stay open. It shows who is in control of the strength.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close cancels huge volume. The close is a gate.
questions.simple: False, because the close must be in the upper half of the range, however big the volume was.

reasons: card gate; the same gate as q12 and q65

questions.q: What volume test does a day-one buy have to pass?
choices: The average daily volume by 10:00
Double the average by the close
Half the average daily volume by 10:00
The average daily volume by lunch
questions.answer: The average daily volume by 10:00
questions.why: The average daily volume by 10:00 Eastern, which is the first 30 minutes. Our card wants the gap day at 3 times the 50-day average volume. By the buy, the full average daily volume must also be on pace to trade within the first 30 minutes. Kullamagi: ideally within 15 to 20 minutes or even quicker. Volume is the number one thing.
questions.lesson_line: On pace means a whole day's volume before the coffee is cold.

wrong.Double the average by the close: Double by the close is a B- day on our card, and it is known too late for a day-one buy.
wrong.The average daily volume by lunch: By lunch is too slow. The test is the first 30 minutes, or quicker.
wrong.Half the average daily volume by 10:00: Half a day is not on pace. Our card wants the full average daily volume within the first 30 minutes.

questions.simple: The full average day of volume must trade in the first 30 minutes, which means by 10:00 Eastern.

deeper.trap: The test is a pace, not a final tally. Kullamagi wants the average daily volume to trade in the first 15 to 20 minutes or even quicker. Our card allows the first 30 minutes, so a stock that reaches it only by 10:00 is on the slow edge of the test.

reasons: card test; Kullamagi's quote agrees

questions.q: How do you rate this second gap?
choices: Weaker; a second EP fails more often
Stronger; the first gap proved the story
The same; every gap starts fresh
Skip it; a contract is not a catalyst
questions.story: Three months ago a stock had a textbook EP: a 14% earnings gap on 4x volume that held. It has run since. Now it gaps 12% on 4x volume on a new contract win.
questions.answer: Weaker; a second EP fails more often
questions.why: Weaker. Kullamagi says a second EP can work, but the failure rate is higher and the move probably will not be as big. Bonde: an EP at the beginning of a move is worth more than a later one. A third or fourth surprise is often priced in. The stock has already been re-priced once.
questions.lesson_line: A second surprise is worth less. The first one already moved the price.

wrong.Stronger; the first gap proved the story: The first gap already moved the stock, so part of the news is in the price. Bonde values an EP at the start of a move more than a later one.
wrong.The same; every gap starts fresh: The stock is no longer overlooked. Kullamagi says a later EP can work, but it fails more and moves less.
wrong.Skip it; a contract is not a catalyst: A contract is a named catalyst, though earnings come first. The problem is the earlier run, not the news.

questions.simple: A second EP is weaker because the stock has already been re-priced once and more of the news is in the price.

deeper.counter: Bonde looks for neglect plus a first or second earnings surprise, so a second gap alone does not end his trade. Kullamagi says an EP after an earlier one can work, but fails more and moves less.

reasons: rests on the card's first-EP line (c06), a held pick
re-asked as the card's test, not as a ban

questions.q: What shows the buyers stayed in control that day?
choices: Closed near its high, gap still open
Closed green, but the gap filled late
Closed near its low after a spike
Closed mid-range; neither side won
questions.answer: Closed near its high, gap still open
questions.why: Closed near its high, with the gap still open. We want bull gaps to stay open. It shows who is in control of the strength. A close near the high says the buyers held the day. A close near the low says sellers took it back and the news is not being believed. This gap closed at 91% of its range.
questions.lesson_line: Strong close, gap open. The buyers were in control all day.

wrong.Closed green, but the gap filled late: A gap that trades back to the prior close is filled and the setup is out, green or not.
wrong.Closed near its low after a spike: A close near the low means sellers took the day back. We want bull gaps to stay open.
wrong.Closed mid-range; neither side won: A close in the middle of the range shows no one in control. We want a strong close with the gap still open.

questions.simple: A close near the high with the gap still open shows buyers held the day. A close near the low means sellers won.

reasons: reworded and fixed before

questions.story: The gap day is the last bar: a 12.1% gap on a deal announcement, on 10.3x volume. Look at where it closed and whether the gap stayed open.

questions.q: The report is out at 7:30 and the stock is up 15% pre-market on big volume. We wait for regular hours.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. No new buys outside regular trading hours. The opening range forms after the bell, and so does the stop under it.
questions.lesson_line: Pre-market shows you the gap. Regular hours give you the trade.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We usually wait until day ___ at the earliest for a first sell.
questions.why: 3. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: First sell: day 3 at the earliest, and it is a judgment call.
questions.simple: We wait until day 3 at the earliest for a first sell, and it is a judgment call.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, first trim)

questions.q: You buy a delayed entry on day three. Where is the stop?
choices: Just under the trigger day's low
Under the gap-day low, it holds
Under the prior close, gap fill
Under the 9 EMA, the trail
questions.answer: Just under the trigger day's low
questions.why: Just under the trigger day's low, by a few cents. Stop first: the size comes from the stop. If price trades under the trigger day's low, the break has failed. A stop just under it keeps a failed break cheap. Morales uses the gap-up day's low as his selling guide, and ours sits at or above it, so ours is tighter. Every position has a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger day's low is the stop. Not the gap-day low, not the base.

wrong.Under the prior close, gap fill: A gap fill is an invalidation before entry, not a stop after it. Far too wide.
wrong.Under the gap-day low, it holds: Morales uses the gap-up day's low as his selling guide. Ours is the trigger day's low, which sits at or above it, so the stop is tighter.
wrong.Under the 9 EMA, the trail: The 9 EMA is the trail for what is left, sold on a close below it. It is not the first stop.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the trigger day's low. If it trades there, the break failed and the loss stays small.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62, stop first)

questions.story: Day two after an earnings gap. Tomorrow it trades over the post-gap high, and you buy that day-three break.

questions.q: Prior close 40.00, today's open 44.80. How big is the gap, in percent?
questions.why: 12.0%. The gap is the open minus the prior close, over the prior close: (44.80 - 40.00) / 40.00 = 12%. Kullamagi defines his EP as a gap up of 10% or more, with big volume by the first minutes after the open. The gap alone does not make an EP: it also needs a named catalyst.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap from the prior close to the open. Then check the volume.
questions.simple: Take the open minus the prior close, divide by the prior close, and you get 12.0%.

reasons: computed key
the gap floor is a held decision (D-033)

wrong.10.7%: Divided the gap by the open, not by the prior close.
wrong.4.8%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.1.2%: A decimal slip. The gap is far more than a percent.

questions.q: Is this an Episodic Pivot?
choices: No; that news is a weak catalyst
Yes; the gap and volume suffice
Yes; any news is the episode
No; the gap is too small
questions.story: A stock gaps up 15% on big volume. The only news is a morning television mention by a well-known host.
questions.answer: No; that news is a weak catalyst
questions.why: No. A media mention or an analyst upgrade alone is a weak catalyst. Bonde: publication mentions and upgrades have a low probability of follow-through, while earnings, new products and raised guidance have a high one. The 15% gap and the volume are only half the setup. The other half is a real episode.
questions.lesson_line: A television mention is not an episode. Earnings, a contract, an approval: those are.

wrong.Yes; the gap and volume suffice: Price and volume are half of the EP. The other half is the news, and a mention is weak news.
wrong.Yes; any news is the episode: Bonde keeps a high-probability list and a low-probability list. Mentions sit on the second.
wrong.No; the gap is too small: A 15% gap clears Kullamagi's line of 10% or more. The catalyst is what fails here.

questions.simple: No. A television mention is weak news, and the setup needs a real episode like earnings or raised guidance.

reasons: rests on the card's catalyst line, a held decision (D-032)

questions.q: Buy, or wait?
choices: Buy at market; stop under the low
Wait for the close to confirm the gap
Wait for a pullback to the gap fill
Buy half now, half at the close
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 14% on earnings, with volume on pace for 6x the average. At 9:40 it trades over the 5-minute high. The low of the day is 2.1% below.
questions.answer: Buy at market; stop under the low
questions.why: Buy at market, with the stop a few cents under the low of the day. The stop is only 2.1% away, inside the 1 to 3% we prefer. So the full size goes in at one price with one stop. Waiting for the close would push the stop far away and shrink the size. Our GRRR note puts the stop at the low of the day too. Heavy volume is a plus, not a must.
questions.lesson_line: A tight low under a holding gap is the day-one buy. Take it.

wrong.Wait for the close to confirm the gap: By the close the stop is far away and the size is tiny. The opening range is the tight entry.
wrong.Wait for a pullback to the gap fill: A gap fill is the invalidation, not the entry. We want the gap to stay open.
wrong.Buy half now, half at the close: The full size goes in at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.simple: Buy at market now, because the stop under the day's low is only 2.1% away and waiting would push it far off.

reasons: the day-one buy is a held decision (D-005)

questions.q: How do you handle this gap day?
choices: Wait for a delayed-entry trigger
Go in with an 8% stop, usual shares
Put the stop 3% under and buy
Wait for the close, then buy
questions.story: A stock gaps 14% on earnings on 6x volume and holds. At 10:00 it trades over the opening-range high, but the low of the day is 8% below the price.
questions.answer: Wait for a delayed-entry trigger
questions.why: Wait for a delayed-entry trigger. The honest stop is a few cents under the day's low, and that is 8% away. The size comes from the stop. So an 8% stop either cuts the shares a lot or risks far more than planned. We prefer stops 1 to 3% away, and up to 5% is acceptable. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger instead of tightening the stop to fit. While the gap holds, a later trigger can still give a stop within 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last. A wide low means wait, not tighten.

wrong.Go in with an 8% stop, usual shares: A stop 8% away is past the 5% we accept. And the usual share count would risk far more than planned, since the size comes from the stop.
wrong.Put the stop 3% under and buy: A stop 3% under sits above the day's low, so you tightened it to fit. We never tighten a stop to fit. We wait for a tighter trigger.
wrong.Wait for the close, then buy: We buy as price trades through a trigger, never at the close. The day's low is still down there, so the stop stays far away.

questions.simple: Wait for the delayed entry. An 8% stop forces a much smaller size or too much risk, and we never tighten a stop to fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13)
held decision D-005 (day-one stop width)

questions.q: What is the read for an EP long?
choices: Step aside; the gap filled
Buy; the fill is support
Buy at the close if it bounces
Short; the gap is dead
questions.story: A stock gaps 12% on earnings. By 11:00 it has traded all the way back to yesterday's close.
questions.answer: Step aside; the gap filled
questions.why: Step aside. A trade back to the prior close on day one fills the gap, and the setup is off. We want bull gaps to stay open because it shows who is in control. A filled gap means the sellers won the day, and a later bounce does not bring the setup back.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fills on day one had no buyers behind it.

wrong.Buy; the fill is support: A filled gap is the invalidation. There is no EP left to buy.
wrong.Buy at the close if it bounces: The fill already ended the setup. A late bounce does not bring it back.
wrong.Short; the gap is dead: The read is to step aside. A filled gap is not a short signal either.

questions.simple: Step aside. Once the stock trades back to yesterday's close the gap has filled, which means the sellers won the day.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: The app's market filter reads Orange. By our guide, which EP can you take?
choices: Only the cleanest, an A+ EP
An A EP, at half the size
None; Orange means all cash
Any EP; EPs ignore the market
questions.answer: Only the cleanest, an A+ EP
questions.why: Only an A+ EP. The market reading is the app's market filter. Green means full risk per grade, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups, Red mostly cash and shorts. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup is, and it sets the size. In a weak market we take only the cleanest setups. Bulkowski buys the earnings breakout only when the market and industry trend higher. It is a guide, not a hard cap.
questions.lesson_line: Orange: only the cleanest setups, the A+ ones.

wrong.Any EP; EPs ignore the market: Bonde finds EPs even in bear markets, but we keep the market filter.
wrong.An A EP, at half the size: Orange filters by grade, not by size. An A is below A+, so it stays out even at half size.
wrong.None; Orange means all cash: Orange still lets the A+ setups through. It is a filter, not a ban.

questions.simple: In an Orange market only the cleanest setups, the A+ ones, get through, because a weak market punishes weaker trades.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.q: Most EPs come in a window of a few weeks each quarter, in earnings season.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Most EPs come in a window of 3 to 4 weeks each quarter. That is when companies report and the surprises arrive together. Kullamagi says they mostly occur in a concentrated period of 3-4 weeks every quarter. Hunt hard in those weeks and be patient between them.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings season is EP season. Keep the list ready before it starts.
questions.simple: True. EPs follow news, and most of the news is earnings, which comes in a few weeks each quarter.

reasons: a count that varies by season (50 to 100)

questions.q: The 50-day average volume is 2 million shares. The gap day traded 5.5 million. What is the multiple?
questions.why: 2.75 times. Divide the gap day's volume by the 50-day average: 5.5 million / 2 million = 2.75. That is under the 3 times our card wants, in the B- row for 2 to 3 times. Bonde's scan asks for 3 times the 50-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. Three times is the floor.
questions.simple: 5.5 million divided by 2 million is 2.75 times, which is under the 3 times our card wants.

reasons: computed key

wrong.3.50x: Took the difference of the two volumes, not the ratio.
wrong.0.36x: Flipped it: the average divided by the gap day's volume.
wrong.7.50x: Added the two volumes instead of dividing.

questions.q: EP or Power Earnings Gap?
choices: A PEG; a leader, not neglected
An EP; the gap and volume qualify
An EP; earnings make it one
A Kicker; it gapped from a base
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. Into the report the stock had climbed 25.5% in six months and sat near its highs. It gaps 16.6% on 11.2x volume and closes at 80% of its range.
questions.answer: A PEG; a leader, not neglected
questions.why: A Power Earnings Gap. An EP needs a neglected stock, and this one had been climbing, up 25.5% over six months and near its highs. It is an established leader gapping on a report, not a forgotten stock being re-priced. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings. Kullamagi: it is best if the stock has not rallied in the past 3 to 6 months. The gap and the volume are strong, but they are only half the test.
questions.lesson_line: Same report, two setups. The six months before the gap decide which.

wrong.An EP; the gap and volume qualify: The gap day is strong, but the stock before it is not neglected. It had already climbed 25.5% in six months.
wrong.An EP; earnings make it one: An earnings gap on a leader at highs is the PEG. The EP is the neglected name's gap.
wrong.A Kicker; it gapped from a base: A Kicker needs a weak red close and a small gap. This one gapped 16.6% on 11.2x volume to a strong close.

questions.simple: It is a Power Earnings Gap, because a stock that already climbed into the report is a leader, not a forgotten name.

reasons: held decision D-002 (earnings gap on a neglected or an established name)
neglect line is a proposed card line

questions.q: Neglect check. The close 126 sessions ago was 20.00 and the close before the gap is 24.00. How far is it up, in percent?
questions.why: 20%. The close before the gap is 24.00 and the close 126 sessions earlier is 20.00. So (24.00 - 20.00) / 20.00 = 20%. Our card's neglect line is at most 25% over 126 sessions, so this passes that half of the test. The card also asks for at most 15% over 63 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Neglect is measured, not felt. Six months back, count how far it has come.
questions.simple: Take 24.00 over 20.00 and subtract one to get the percent up. That is 20%, under the 25% neglect line.

deeper.example: CRM, August 2020, was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63. Both are past the card's lines of 25% and 15%, so it was not neglected. It was an established leader at highs, not an EP.

reasons: computed key
rests on a proposed card line (ep.neglect)

wrong.120.0%: Gave the ratio and forgot to subtract one.
wrong.16.7%: Divided the rise by the later close, not the earlier one.
wrong.4.0%: Used the dollar rise as if it were the percent.

questions.q: How do you trade this morning's break?
choices: Buy at market; stop under today's low
Pass; day one was the only entry
Buy; stop under the gap-day low
Wait for a pullback to the prior close
questions.story: An earnings gap of 20.3% on 27.6x volume closed at 82% of its range two days ago. Yesterday it held above the gap-day low. This morning it trades over the post-gap high, and the stop under today's low would sit 1.7% below.
questions.answer: Buy at market; stop under today's low
questions.why: Buy at market as it trades over the post-gap high, with the stop a few cents under the trigger day's low. The gap held: nothing traded below the gap-day low, so the buyers are still in control. The stop is only 1.7% away, inside the 1 to 3% we prefer, so a failed break costs little. If the honest stop were past 5%, we would wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Miss day one and the break of the gap-day high, while the gap holds, is the second door.

wrong.Pass; day one was the only entry: The delayed entry is our second trigger. While the gap holds, the first break of the post-gap high is a buy.
wrong.Buy; stop under the gap-day low: The stop is a few cents under the trigger day's low. The gap-day low is wider than it needs to be.
wrong.Wait for a pullback to the prior close: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap and ends the setup. That is not a pullback to buy.

questions.simple: Buy at market over the post-gap high with the stop under today's low. The gap held, so a failed break costs little.

deeper.example: ENPH, October 2021: an 18.5% earnings gap closed at 56% of its range. On day three it broke the post-gap high, 227.59. The buy was 227.60 with the stop at 224.95, 1.2% under.

reasons: the delayed-entry window is a held decision (D-084)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62)

questions.q: Under our rule for a gap through the stop, where is the stop now?
choices: 29.00, the first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, 29.20
No stop until it reclaims 29.40
Get out; the gap is past 2R
questions.story: You bought an EP at 30.00 with the stop at 29.40. Follow-up news gaps it open at 29.20, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 29.00.
questions.answer: 29.00, the first 30-minute low
questions.why: 29.00. When a stock gaps through your stop, the first 30 minutes of that day decide the exit. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. A 2R ceiling caps the damage: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you get out. The original risk was the distance from 30.00 to 29.40, and a loss out to 29.00 is less than twice that, so 29.00 stands.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your stop gets the first 30 minutes to decide, not the open.

wrong.Sell at the open, 29.20: The gap rule gives it the first 30 minutes. The open is not the decision; the 30-minute low is.
wrong.No stop until it reclaims 29.40: Every position has a real stop order with the broker. The new stop is the 30-minute low.
wrong.Get out; the gap is past 2R: The 30-minute low sits inside the 2R ceiling. The ceiling has not been hit.

questions.simple: 29.00 is the new stop, the first 30-minute low. That loss is still under twice the risk you planned, so you stay in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
computed key (the 2R ceiling check)

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Pass; too far past the trigger
Buy; the breakout is confirmed
Buy; the stop just moves up with it
Buy half size to be safe
questions.story: A gap day. The opening-range high was 50.00. You were away from the desk, and at 10:05 the stock trades 52.60.
questions.answer: Pass; too far past the trigger
questions.why: Pass. The buy point is the opening-range high, 50.00, and we never buy more than 4% above it. At 52.60 the fill is past that line. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the day's low, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy; the breakout is confirmed: Confirmed and too far are both true. The chase line is 4% over the trigger.
wrong.Buy; the stop just moves up with it: The stop is the low of the day; it does not follow your late fill. The distance grows and the size shrinks.
wrong.Buy half size to be safe: Half of a chased entry is still a chased entry.

questions.simple: Pass, because 52.60 is more than 4% above the 50.00 opening-range high, and chasing shrinks your size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
computed key (52.60 against the 4% line)

questions.q: Three green days in a row before the delayed trigger is a reason to wait. A guide, not a gate.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card says not after three green days in a row. It is a guide, not a gate, so it is a reason to wait and not a ban.
questions.lesson_line: After three green days in a row, wait. It is a guide, not a gate.
questions.simple: True. After three green days in a row our card says wait, though it is a guide and not a firm ban.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on a proposed card line (ep.not_three_green)

questions.q: If the average daily volume has not traded by the first 30 minutes, the day-one buy is off.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The volume is not there by the first 30 minutes: an invalidation on day one. Kullamagi: ideally the average daily volume trades in the first 15-20 minutes or quicker.
questions.lesson_line: No crowd in the first 30 minutes, no day-one buy. The gap is only a gap.

questions.q: Take the opening-range buy?
choices: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
No; a contract is not a real catalyst
Yes; the gap day's volume is huge
Yes; Bonde wanted a small float
questions.story: A $7 stock that trades about $4 million a day gaps 20% on a contract. Even on the gap day it trades $9 million.
questions.answer: No; under $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one is at $7 and trades about $4 million a day, and even its $9 million gap day falls short. The point is the exit as much as the entry. A stock that trades this little is hard to get in and out of at your price. Bonde prefers a small float, which is a different thing from dollars traded.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect EP in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.Yes; the gap day's volume is huge: Huge for this stock is still $9 million, under our $20 million a day line.
wrong.No; a contract is not a real catalyst: A contract is a named catalyst. This stock fails on price and dollar volume, not on the news.
wrong.Yes; Bonde wanted a small float: Bonde prefers a small float, which is not the same as dollars traded. Our $10 and $20 million rule comes first.

questions.simple: No. A stock this thin is hard to get in and out of, and it fails our $10 and $20 million a day tests.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, liquidity), a held decision (D-030)

questions.q: Bought at 514.01 with the stop at 507.19. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $534.47. One R is the fill minus the stop: 514.01 minus 507.19. Add three of those to the fill, 514.01, and you get 534.47. 3R is a measuring mark, not a fixed sell. UI reached 3R the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R price before the open. It is a measuring mark, not a sell order.
questions.simple: One R is the gap between your fill and your stop. Add three of those to the fill to find 3R.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$527.65: Added the three R to the stop instead of the fill.
wrong.$493.55: Subtracted the three R instead of adding them.

questions.story: Bought on the day-two break after an earnings gap.

questions.q: On an EP our rulebook ideally moves the stop to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We move the stop up to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R, ideally, or at the first sell. At breakeven a pullback can no longer turn the trade into a loss. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Move the stop to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R. The rest rides with little at risk.
questions.simple: True. The stop may move to breakeven from 2R to 5R, so a pullback cannot turn the winner into a loss.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
reworded: the old 'by default at the first trim' had no source

questions.q: What happens to what is left?
choices: Sold on a close under the 9 EMA
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Held until the gap-day low breaks
Added; the dip is the entry
questions.story: Your EP has moved fast, riding above its 9 EMA for three weeks. You sold part into the push on the way up. Today it closes under the 9 EMA for the first time.
questions.answer: Sold on a close under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Sold. A fast mover trails the 9 EMA, and a close below it sells what is left. Falling under the 9 EMA for the first time says the fast run is over, so you keep most of the gain. You already sold part into the push. Kullamagi trails the 10- or 20-day average. We use the 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Part banked, what is left rides the 9 EMA. The close below it is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is a floor for the stop, not the exit plan. The trail is the exit for what is left.
wrong.Added; the dip is the entry: Full size at one price with one stop, and no adding. A close under the trail is an exit.
wrong.Held until the gap-day low breaks: The trail, not the gap-day low, is the exit for what is left, and it sits much closer to price.

questions.simple: Sell it. A close under the 9 EMA says the fast run is over, so you keep most of the gain.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi trails the 10- or 20-day average. We use the 9 EMA for a fast mover and the 20 EMA for a steadier one. The lines are close but not the same, so know which one your plan names before the stock moves.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)
held decision D-024 (the trail line)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Sell; under 1R after 10 trading days
Hold; the stop has not been hit
Hold; the next report lifts it
Sell half now, trail the rest
questions.story: You bought a delayed EP entry. Ten trading days later it sits at 0.4R, never near 3R, never near the stop.
questions.answer: Sell; under 1R after 10 trading days
questions.why: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money. This one sits at 0.4R. Bonde was stricter: the stock should move within 5 days or you go on to the next opportunity. The stop is a separate exit and does not replace the clock.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and no progress: the trade has had its chance. Free the money.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: The stop is one exit; the time stop is another. Ten days under 1R is the second.
wrong.Hold; the next report lifts it: A hoped-for report is not part of this trade's plan. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.
wrong.Sell half now, trail the rest: The time stop sells the whole trade. Trailing the rest is for after the trims.

questions.simple: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold, and this one is at 0.4R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)
ours and Bonde's clocks differ

questions.q: A+, A, B or B-?
choices: B- at best; over 25%
A+; everything else is perfect
A; the volume saves it
No trade; a gap that big is banned
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 32% on 20x volume and closes at the high, the first such day in a year.
questions.answer: B- at best; over 25%
questions.why: B- at best. A gap over 25% is graded down, not banned. Bonde: if the gaps are more than 20% the stocks pull back most of the time; smaller gaps are better.
questions.lesson_line: The biggest gaps are often one-day moves. Size them small.

wrong.A+; everything else is perfect: The rest is A+ and the gap size is not. The grade is the weakest line.
wrong.A; the volume saves it: Volume grades the day up, the gap size grades it down. The card calls it B- at best.
wrong.No trade; a gap that big is banned: Graded down, not banned. The card's own words are B- at best.

questions.q: Which earnings report makes the stronger case?
choices: The first; stronger growth and a raise
The second; steady growth lasts longer
Equal; a beat is all that matters
Neither; growth does not matter
questions.story: Two earnings EPs. One reports sales up 140% with a beat and raised guidance. The other reports sales and earnings both up 20%, with a beat.
questions.answer: The first; stronger growth and a raise
questions.why: The first. Faster growth and a raised outlook give the new price more to stand on. Kullamagi: ideally triple digit year over year earnings and sales growth, but mid to high double digits works really well too. Bonde tracked only companies with earnings up 100% or more. We prefer growing sales and earnings, and the chart comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Faster growth and a raised outlook make the stronger earnings case.

wrong.The second; steady growth lasts longer: Slower growth gives the new price less to stand on. Kullamagi wants ideally triple-digit growth, though mid to high double digits works too.
wrong.Equal; a beat is all that matters: A beat on 20% growth is weaker than 140% growth with a raised outlook. Growth is not a gate, but more of it is better.
wrong.Neither; growth does not matter: We prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings, though the chart comes first.

questions.simple: The first report is stronger. Sales up 140% with a raised outlook gives the new price more to stand on.

reasons: rests on proposed grading cues (c09)
grading is discretionary (E50), so the stem asks for the card's cues

questions.q: Hold, add or sell into the run?
choices: Sell a big part into the strength
Hold; the trail is the only exit
Add; momentum is strongest here
Sell everything at the open tomorrow
questions.story: Your EP is up 6R after five straight up days, two of them gap ups, each day's range wider than the last.
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. After five straight up days with wider ranges, 6R is in hand. A burst like this often marks the end of the move. A climax run on your own long is Bracco's parabolic burst: sell a big part into it, a judgment call. ChartSchool notes that exhaustion gaps happen near the end of a good trend. Selling into strength banks the gain while buyers are still there.
questions.lesson_line: When your EP goes vertical, sell into the strength. The trail will be too late.

wrong.Hold; the trail is the only exit: The trail is the default. A climax is the exception the rulebook names.
wrong.Add; momentum is strongest here: Our rule is one price, one stop, no adding. Adding into a climax run is chasing.
wrong.Sell everything at the open tomorrow: The rule says a big part, not everything, and into the strength rather than waiting for tomorrow's open.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the run. Bursts like this often end fast, so you bank the gain while buyers are still there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), a judgment call

questions.q: Which of the two is the better EP?
choices: The flat one; the other already ran
The one up 70%; strength begets strength
Neither; a 12% gap is too small
Both equal; the gap day is identical
questions.story: Two 12% earnings gaps on 5x volume, both closing strong. One stock was flat for eight months. The other was already up 70% in the last six months.
questions.answer: The flat one; the other already ran
questions.why: The flat one. A stock that already ran has priced much of the news in. A flat one has not. Kullamagi: it is best if the stock has not rallied over the past 3 to 6 months. Bonde: an EP at the beginning of a move is worth more than a later one. The gap day is the same for both. The six months before it is what separates them.
questions.lesson_line: Same gap, same volume, different value. The six months before decide.

wrong.The one up 70%; strength begets strength: A stock that already ran is no longer overlooked. Bonde values an EP at the start of a move more than a later one.
wrong.Neither; a 12% gap is too small: A 12% gap is plenty big for an EP. The six months before the gap is what separates these two.
wrong.Both equal; the gap day is identical: The gap day is the same and the context is not. Kullamagi wants a stock that has not rallied in the past 3 to 6 months.

questions.simple: The flat stock is the better EP, because the one already up 70% had run before the news and is worth less.

deeper.example: Two names, one report. The flat stock was still overlooked going in. The one up 70% had already been bid up, so the news landed on a stock that was no longer overlooked. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings.

reasons: provisional card reading of the up-50% row (picked 2026-11-10)

questions.q: $40,000 account, 0.5% risk. Fill 34.89, stop 33.96. How many shares?
questions.answer: 215 shares
questions.why: 215 shares. Stop first: the size comes from the stop. Risk in dollars is 40,000 x 0.5%. Risk per share is the fill minus the stop: 34.89 - 33.96. Divide the first by the second and round down to 215. Sizing from the stop means a wider stop gets fewer shares. So a trade stopped at its stop costs about 0.5% of the account, unless a gap jumps the stop. The position stays under the 40% cap.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop sets the size, so divide the dollars you risk by the gap to the stop and round down to 215.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
fixed before (the cap broke at 1% risk)

choices: 430 shares
2,150 shares
215 shares
5 shares

wrong.430 shares: Used twice the stated risk percent.
wrong.2,150 shares: Decimal slip: the risk dollars came out ten times too big.
wrong.5 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the fill price, not the gap to the stop.

questions.story: Bought on the day-three break of the post-gap high.

questions.q: EP or High Volume Edge?
choices: An HVE; record volume with no gap
An EP; record volume is enough
Neither; up 9% is too small
An EP; it closed in the upper half
questions.story: A stock closes up 9% on the most shares it has ever traded in a day. It opened flat; there was no gap.
questions.answer: An HVE; record volume with no gap
questions.why: A High Volume Edge. An HVE is a record-volume up day, gap or no gap. An EP needs the gap, because the gap is what shows the news re-priced the stock before the open. Record volume also shows on EP days, per Bonde, so the gap is what separates the two.
questions.lesson_line: Record volume without a gap is an HVE. The gap is what makes the EP.

wrong.An EP; record volume is enough: Volume is one half. The EP is an opening gap on volume; this one opened flat.
wrong.Neither; up 9% is too small: The size of the day is not the issue. It is an HVE day, a level to mark.
wrong.An EP; it closed in the upper half: A strong close is not enough. An EP also needs a big gap, and this day opened flat.

questions.simple: It is a High Volume Edge. An EP needs the overnight gap that shows the news re-priced the stock, and this day opened flat.

reasons: card tell between two setups

questions.q: EP or Kicker?
choices: A Kicker; no catalyst, a small gap
An EP; the gap holds all day
An EP; the red close is the neglect
Neither; a gap needs a catalyst
questions.story: A stock closes weak and red. The next morning it gaps 2% up on no news and keeps going.
questions.answer: A Kicker; no catalyst, a small gap
questions.why: A Kicker. A Kicker needs a weak red close, then a small gap up the next morning, rarely on earnings. This one came on no news. An EP is a re-pricing by a named catalyst, and the prior day can be any color. With no named catalyst there is no EP.
questions.lesson_line: Look at the day before and name the news. No news, small gap: a Kicker.

wrong.An EP; the red close is the neglect: One red day is not six months of neglect. The red close is the Kicker's tell.
wrong.An EP; the gap holds all day: A holding gap is not enough. An EP needs a named catalyst, and this one had no news.
wrong.Neither; a gap needs a catalyst: A Kicker does not need a catalyst. It is its own setup, rarely on earnings.

questions.simple: It is a Kicker: a weak red close, then a small gap. With no news it cannot be an EP, which needs a named catalyst.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: EP or News Failure?
choices: A News Failure; no long here
An EP; the gap and the news qualify
An EP; buy the day-2 reclaim
Nothing; wait for the next report
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 12% on a strong report, sells off all day on heavy volume, and closes under yesterday's close.
questions.answer: A News Failure; no long here
questions.why: A News Failure. An EP holds its gap and closes strong. A News Failure gaps up on good news and closes red, under the prior close. Same headline, opposite read. The stock closed under yesterday's close. Every buyer from the gap is under water, and there is no gap left to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Read the close against the prior close. Red on good news is the failure.

wrong.An EP; the gap and the news qualify: The gap and the news were there and the close erased both. A gap that sells off is not an EP.
wrong.An EP; buy the day-2 reclaim: There is no gap left to reclaim. The day closed under the prior close.
wrong.Nothing; wait for the next report: It is something: a News Failure, a read that leans the other way.

questions.simple: It is a News Failure, because the gap sold off and closed under the prior close, the reverse of an EP.

reasons: card tell between two setups

questions.q: Bonde says an EP can only come from a young, small, low-float company.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Bonde says the most explosive EPs come from young companies under $10 billion. He also says widely covered companies do not do as well. That makes small, young names the best hunting ground, not the only one. A larger name can still be an EP, provided it was neglected and the surprise is real.
questions.lesson_line: Young and small names run hardest, but they are not the only EPs.
questions.simple: False. Young, small names run hardest, but a larger neglected name with a real surprise can still be an EP.

deeper.counter: Bonde also says earnings breakouts on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well. That is a tilt toward small names, not a ban on large ones.

reasons: cue, not a gate; two sources agree

questions.q: How many do you take in the first week?
choices: A few; add more as they work
All six; Green is full risk
None; wait for indexes to confirm
One; EPs are risky in a correction
questions.story: A correction just ended and the app's market filter turned Green, which allows full risk. Earnings season is on, and six neglected names gapped on reports this week.
questions.answer: A few; add more as they work
questions.why: A few. After a market correction the filter turns Green and allows full risk. We still start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. That keeps a false start cheap. Bonde: after months of correction you find 50 to 100 opportunities in an earnings season, so there is no need to take them all at once.
questions.lesson_line: A few first, more as they work. A false start then costs little.

wrong.All six; Green is full risk: Full risk is the ceiling, not the first week's order. Earn the next positions.
wrong.None; wait for indexes to confirm: The Green filter already is the market's confirmation. Bonde finds EP opportunities even in bear markets, so waiting longer can miss the leaders.
wrong.One; EPs are risky in a correction: One is too few. After a correction we start with a few positions, and nothing in the story makes these names riskier than usual.

questions.simple: Take a few. After a correction you start small and add as the first ones work, so a false start costs little.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading Green as all in. Green allows full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Right after a correction, our rule starts you with a few and adds only as the first ones work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68)

questions.q: What is the right read of this loss?
choices: A loss from a strong gap that failed
A loss from a stop set too tight
A loss from a gap too big to buy
A loss from a gap on thin volume
questions.story: A big name gaps 18.2% on 13.1x volume when it names a new CEO, closing at 98% of its range. Day four, an inside-day break at 94.97, stop 92.93. The next day takes the stop.
questions.answer: A loss from a strong gap that failed
questions.why: A loss from a strong gap that failed. The gap on 13.1x volume and a 98% close were strong, but there was no follow-through. A strong gap can still fail, and the stop is what keeps that failure small: it held the loss near 1R. A loss taken at the plan is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A strong gap can still fail to follow through. The stop keeps the loss small.

wrong.A loss from a stop set too tight: A few cents under the trigger day's low is our rule. It kept the loss near 1R, which is the plan.
wrong.A loss from a gap too big to buy: A big gap that holds and closes near its high is the picture we want. The size was not the problem.
wrong.A loss from a gap on thin volume: 13.1x the average is heavy volume. The volume was not the problem.

questions.simple: A stop-out is a planned loss. A strong gap can still fail, and the stop kept this loss to about 1R.

deeper.example: SBUX, 2024-08-13: an 18.2% gap on 13.1x volume on the new-CEO news, closing at 98% of its range. The day-4 break at 94.97 with the stop at 92.93 was stopped the next day, and its best run was 0.0R. The stop made the loss cheap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4 and B21)
dossier scan numbers (28% and 41%)
reworded before

questions.q: What is the lesson?
choices: Right stock; the first buy failed
Re-buy at once; stop was wrong
Drop the stock; it failed once
The stop should have been wider
questions.story: A 17.2% earnings gap on 4.4x volume. You buy the day-3 break of the post-gap high at 22.01, stop 21.46. The next session takes the stop. Months later the stock makes a far larger move.
questions.answer: Right stock; the first buy failed
questions.why: Right stock, the first buy failed. The day-3 break failed at once, and the stop kept the loss near 1R, so it cost little. A stop-out says nothing final about the stock: TSLA made a far larger move months later. After a stop-out we buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Buying back at once is hope, not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the stock. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Re-buy at once; stop was wrong: After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop. A re-buy at once is not a new trigger.
wrong.Drop the stock; it failed once: A stop-out says nothing final about the stock. TSLA made a far larger move months later.
wrong.The stop should have been wider: A few cents under the trigger day's low is the rule, and a wider stop only risks more. The stop kept the loss near 1R, which is its job.

questions.simple: The stock was right but the first buy failed. A stop-out is not a verdict, and a new trigger is a new trade.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging the stock by one trade. TSLA, 2019-10-24: the day-3 break at 22.01 was stopped the next session, 0.0R, yet the stock went on to a far larger move months later. The trade can fail while the idea is right. You wait for the next trigger instead of chasing or giving up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: What was the weakest point of this setup?
choices: The run it made before the report
The size of the earnings gap
The volume on the gap day
Where it closed in the day's range
questions.story: A 13.0% earnings gap on 7.4x volume, closing at 86%, on a stock up 19% over the prior six months. The day-3 break at 35.16 reaches 0.51R, then the stop at 34.16 goes.
questions.answer: The run it made before the report
questions.why: The run it made before the report. The stock was up 19% over the prior six months, the least neglected of the four failures in our scan. A stock that already rose has priced part of the news in. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings. The gap, volume and close were all strong. A soft spot is not a proven cause. The day-3 break reached 0.5R and gave it back. The stop kept the loss near 1R.
questions.lesson_line: A trade can pass every rule and still fail. The stop keeps it small.

wrong.The volume on the gap day: 7.4x the average is heavy volume. The volume was not the problem.
wrong.The size of the earnings gap: 13.0% is a big gap. The size was not the problem.
wrong.Where it closed in the day's range: 86% of the range means it closed near its high. The close was strong.

questions.simple: The weakest point was the 19% run before the report, which had already priced in part of the news.

deeper.trap: Passing every rule is not a promise of a win. GOOGL, 2015-07-17: a 13.0% gap on 7.4x volume, closing at 86%, yet up 19% into the news and the least neglected of the four failures. It reached 0.51R and gave it back. The stop made it a small loss.

reasons: soft label: the card's up-50% row does not apply to +19%
fixed before

questions.q: By the card's grade line, how do you size that trade?
choices: Small; B- at best, so sized down
Full; neglect plus volume is A+
Sized up; the biggest gaps run most
Not at all; a 28.5% gap is banned
questions.story: A stock down 31% over six months gaps 28.5% on earnings on 15.0x volume, closing at 97%. You buy the day-2 break at 42.01, stop 40.97.
questions.answer: Small; B- at best, so sized down
questions.why: Small. A gap over 25% is graded down to B- at best, and a B- or lower is sized down. Here the gap was 28.5%. The neglect was textbook, with the stock down 31% over six months, but the gap size was the warning. Bonde also says gaps over 20% pull back most of the time. A big gap is graded down, not banned.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. A B- EP gets a small position.

wrong.Full; neglect plus volume is A+: The gap over 25% caps the grade at B- at best, and B- is sized down.
wrong.Not at all; a 28.5% gap is banned: Graded down, not banned. Small size is the answer, not no trade.
wrong.Sized up; the biggest gaps run most: Bonde: gaps over 20% pull back most of the time. Smaller gaps are better.

questions.simple: Small. A gap over 25% grades no higher than B-, and a B- trade is sized down.

deeper.trap: Good neglect does not lift a big gap. ANF was down 31% over six months and closed at 97% on 15.0x volume. Yet the 28.5% gap was over the 25% line, and it reversed the next session. One example does not prove the rule. It shows why the grade is lower.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.gap_too_big)
the scan runs against the line
answer over 30 characters

questions.q: Is it an EP?
choices: No; a faded day, a watch at most
Yes; the gap held, so it counts
Yes; buy the close, the gap is support
No; the day's volume was too light
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. An 18.1% earnings gap on 4.6x volume. The day never trades back to the prior close, but it closes at 32% of its range.
questions.answer: No; a faded day, a watch at most
questions.why: No. The gap held, but the day closed at 32% of its range, in the lower third. Buyers pushed it up at the open and sellers took the day back, so no one was in control at the close. A faded gap day is not an EP. At most it goes on the list as a delayed-reaction watch. We want bull gaps to stay open and strong.
questions.lesson_line: The gap held and the buyers left. That is a watch, not a buy.

wrong.Yes; buy the close, the gap is support: We buy as price trades through a trigger, not at the close. A held gap with a weak close is not an EP.
wrong.Yes; the gap held, so it counts: Holding the gap is only one test. The close matters too, and this one closed near its low.
wrong.No; the day's volume was too light: 4.6x is heavy volume. The close is what fails.

questions.simple: It is not an EP. The gap held, but the day closed near its low, so the sellers took the day back.

deeper.trap: MU, 2024-09-26: the gap held, since the low of 107.53 stayed above the prior close of 95.77, so a quick look says EP. The close at 32% of the range says the buyers left. Both must hold: the gap stays open and the close is strong.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: Take the day-2 break?
choices: No; the buy is under the 200-day
No; the 66% close is too weak to buy
Yes; the gap and volume qualify
Yes; the 200-day is about to turn up
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. A stock down 17% over six months gaps 12.1% on earnings on 3.6x, closing at 66%. The day-2 break would fill at 161.21. The 200-day sits at 168.35.
questions.answer: No; the buy is under the 200-day
questions.why: No. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. The 200-day marks the long-term trend, and a stock under it is in a downtrend. The one exception is for indexes and ETFs built to move faster than an index, never for a stock. The day-2 break would fill at 161.21, under the 200-day at 168.35. The gap and the volume passed. The location failed.
questions.lesson_line: A neglected stock can sit under its 200-day. No long until price is over it.

wrong.Yes; the gap and volume qualify: The gap day passed. The location failed: no longs below the 200-day.
wrong.Yes; the 200-day is about to turn up: The rule is price above the 200-day at the buy, not an average that may turn later.
wrong.No; the 66% close is too weak to buy: A 66% close is a solid close, not the problem. The buy being under the 200-day is.

questions.simple: No. A stock under its 200-day is in a downtrend, and below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks.

deeper.trap: Neglected stocks often live under the 200-day, so this rule can say no to a gap that looks perfect. The test is price at the buy, not the picture of the gap day. AMZN, 2022-02-04: a 12.1% gap on 3.6x, closed at 66%, and the break at 161.21 was stopped, 0.0R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
a held decision (D-020)

questions.q: EP or Power Earnings Gap?
choices: A PEG; not neglected
An EP; the gap and volume are A+
An EP; 25.5% is close enough
Neither; a leader cannot gap
questions.story: A software leader near its highs gaps 16.6% on earnings on 11.2x volume, closing at 80%. It was up 25.5% over the prior 126 sessions and 19.3% over the prior 63.
questions.answer: A PEG; not neglected
questions.why: A Power Earnings Gap. Up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63; the neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. An established leader at highs gapping on a report is the PEG.
questions.lesson_line: A leader at highs gapping on earnings is a PEG. Measure the six months to know.

wrong.An EP; the gap and volume are A+: The day is A+ for either setup. The stock before it decides, and it was not neglected.
wrong.An EP; 25.5% is close enough: Close enough is over, and the 63-session line fails by more. Measured, not eyeballed.
wrong.Neither; a leader cannot gap: Leaders gap on reports all the time. That is the PEG.

questions.q: Bought at 227.60 with the stop at 224.95. It trades 235.55. Where does that leave the trade?
questions.answer: Up 3.0R; breakeven stop is allowed
questions.why: Up 3.0R, so the stop may go to breakeven. One R is the fill minus the stop: 227.60 - 224.95. The gain per share is 235.55 - 227.60. So (235.55 - 227.60) / (227.60 - 224.95) = 3.0. We may move the stop up to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R. At breakeven a pullback can no longer turn the trade into a loss. ENPH got there the session after the day-3 entry.
questions.lesson_line: Count the gain in R. From 2R to 5R the stop may move to breakeven.
questions.simple: Divide the gain per share by the risk per share to get 3.0R. In that range the stop may go to breakeven.

deeper.trap: 3R is a measuring mark, not a sell signal. The first sell is a judgment, and we very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, first trim)

choices: Up 3.0R; breakeven stop is allowed
Up 8.0R; time to sell it all
Up 4.0R; far too early for breakeven
Up 0.3R; too early to move the stop

wrong.Up 8.0R; time to sell it all: That is the dollar gain without dividing by one R. And the first sell is a judgment, not a rule.
wrong.Up 4.0R; far too early for breakeven: That measured the gain from the stop, not from the fill.
wrong.Up 0.3R; too early to move the stop: That flipped the division: one R over the gain.

questions.story: Bought on the day-three break after an earnings gap.

questions.q: How do we take the first profit on the way up?
choices: A judgment call, usually day 3 or later
A fixed third at 3R, the day it hits
Everything at 3R, the first target
Nothing; hold all of it for the big run
questions.story: A news EP after the election: a 14.2% gap on 3.9x, the day-3 break bought at 259.70, stop 257.10. It reaches 3R the next session, and later 34R.
questions.answer: A judgment call, usually day 3 or later
questions.why: A judgment call, usually day 3 or later. We very rarely sell on day 1 of a buy. A 3, 5 or 7 day push, or about 5 to 10R, is often the best place to sell. That is when the stock is handing you strength. COIN gave its gains back in December after 34R, so selling part into strength mattered.
questions.lesson_line: Sell part into strength, on judgment. An EP that gives it all back only hurts the untrimmed.

wrong.Everything at 3R, the first target: Selling everything in the first day or two and missing the multi-week trend is a named mistake.
wrong.Nothing; hold all of it for the big run: COIN gave its gains back in December after 34R. Selling part into strength mattered.
wrong.A fixed third at 3R, the day it hits: That is a fixed sell at 3R. The first sell is a judgment, and we rarely sell on day 1.

questions.simple: We sell on judgment. COIN gave back its gains after 34R, so we sell part into a 3, 5 or 7 day push.

deeper.trap: The 34R figure is a trap. It was the peak, not a plan. No one knows the peak in advance, so we sell part into strength on judgment and trail the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
the owner often waits for 5R on the first trim

questions.q: What kept this trade a win?
choices: The trims and the 10-day trail
Holding the original stop
Widening the stop to give it room
Selling everything at 3R
questions.story: You bought the day-3 break at 227.60, stop 224.95. 3R came the next session. Weeks later the stock tops, rolls over and collapses through your original stop.
questions.answer: The trims and the 10-day trail
questions.why: The trims and the 10-day trail. A third comes off at 3R and a third at 5R. The last third trails the 10-day while the stock moves fast. This stock topped and collapsed through the original stop, so a plan with only that stop gives the move back. It was ENPH, bought 2021-10-29 at 227.60, and its best run reached 20.7R.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers get the 10-day. By the time the stop is hit, two thirds are gone.

wrong.Holding the original stop: Holding only the original stop means the whole position exits at the stop, so the gain is given back.
wrong.Selling everything at 3R: A third comes off at 3R. Selling everything misses the run to 20.7R and the multi-week trend.
wrong.Widening the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. A looser stop does not bank anything.

questions.simple: The trims and the 10-day trail kept it a win, because they banked gains before the stock fell through the stop.

deeper.example: ENPH: the buy was 227.60 with the stop at 224.95, only 1.2% away, and 3R came the next session. Later the stock topped and collapsed through that stop, yet its best run reached 20.7R. A plan with trims banked part of that run. A plan with one stop gave it back.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52 and B19)
held decision D-024 (the trail line)

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
No; hold through only if up 3R
Yes; the last report was a surprise

questions.q: What is the trade?
choices: Buy; stop under the inside-day low
Pass; day three is too late
Buy; stop under the gap-day low

questions.story: A stock gaps 12.0% on earnings on 5.7x. Two days hold above the gap-day low. Day three is an inside day, trading inside day two's range. Day four it trades over the inside day's high, 59.91, and the inside day's low is 2.3% below.
questions.answer: Buy; stop under the inside-day low
questions.why: Buy at market over the inside day's high, with the stop a few cents under the inside day's low, as WING did. The gap held for two days, so the delayed trigger is live. wrong.Wait for the gap-day high break: That is the other trigger. The inside-day break came first, with a tighter stop.

choices: Record volume; buyers piled in
Ordinary volume; a small event
Light volume; few buyers cared

questions.why: Record volume. The bar on the gap day towers over the year before it. It traded 27.6x the average, the highest volume on the chart by far. Bonde: a genuine surprise leads to a big gap and huge pre-market volume, often the highest in the stock's history. We say volume raises the grade, our judgment of how clean the setup is, but it is not a requirement.
questions.lesson_line: Huge volume is what a real surprise looks like.

wrong.Ordinary volume; a small event: The volume bar towers over the year before it: 27.6x the average, the highest on the chart by far. It was not ordinary.
wrong.Light volume; few buyers cared: 27.6x its average is the opposite of light.
wrong.It adds nothing; only price counts: Volume is what a real surprise looks like. We say it raises the grade, but it is not a must-have.

questions.simple: Record volume shows a real surprise. We say volume raises the grade, but it is not a must-have.

deeper.trap: Do not read volume as a forecast. DLB is the loudest case here and ran 17.1R, but big volume promises nothing about the next one.

questions.q: What do you do on day five?
choices: Hold; the stop and the clock decide
Sell; five flat days is a failed trade
Move the stop up to breakeven right now
Hold, but add as it builds a base
questions.story: A news gap of 12.1% on 10.3x. You bought the day-2 break at 94.17, stop 93.17. Five days later it has gone nowhere, still above the stop.
questions.answer: Hold; the stop and the clock decide
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit, and the time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. At day five neither has fired. SIG stalled a week above the stop and reached 3R on day 8, a patient trade that paid. Bonde's stricter 5-day clock is his rule, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Sideways above the stop is not a loss. Let the rules, not boredom, make the exit.

wrong.Sell; five flat days is a failed trade: Bonde used 5 days. Our time stop is 10 trading days under 1R.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven right now: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, ideally. This trade has not moved.
wrong.Hold, but add as it builds a base: The full size goes in at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.simple: Hold. A trade still under 1R is sold after 10 trading days, and at day five the stop is not hit.

deeper.trap: Patience has a limit. SIG reached 3R on day 8, but the same flat picture past day 10 and under 1R means sell. The stop and the clock are the rules, not a hunch that it will go.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)
ours and Bonde's clocks differ

questions.q: The gap day is the last bar. Read the months before it and the gap day. Buy a delayed break, or pass?
choices: Take it; neglect, strong close
Pass; it was already up
Pass; the gap day closed weak
Take it, but after the fill
questions.answer: Take it; neglect, strong close
questions.why: Take it. The months before the gap show a stock down 19% over six months. That is the neglect the setup needs, so the news had not been priced in. The gap day closed near its high, at 85% of its range, so the buyers held the day. A break over the post-gap high while the gap holds is the delayed trigger, and this one came on day 4. The real numbers: a 10.5% gap on 7.4x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Months of nothing, then a gap that holds. That is the picture to memorise.

wrong.Pass; it was already up: Look left: the stock was down 19% over six months. That is the neglect the EP needs.
wrong.Pass; the gap day closed weak: The gap day closed at 85% of its range, near its high. The close is strong.
wrong.Take it, but after the fill: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap and ends the setup. We step aside then, we do not buy.

questions.simple: Take it. The stock was down for months, then gapped and closed near its high, so a delayed break is a valid buy.

deeper.trap: Look left before you look at the gap. A prior run-up, a weak close or a gap that fills would change the answer.

choices: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
Take it; the gap day is A+
Take it; 25.5% is close enough
Pass; the gap day closed too weak
questions.answer: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
questions.why: Pass as an EP. The stock was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63, and our neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. questions.lesson_line: A big gap on a leader at highs is a PEG. The six months before say so.

wrong.Pass; the gap day closed too weak: The gap day closed at 80% of its range, in the upper half. The close passes and the neglect is what fails.

questions.q: After a delayed-entry buy, the stop can be moved down to the gap-day low.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The size was set from the first stop, so a lower stop risks more than the plan allowed. The delayed entry's stop is a few cents under the trigger day's low, and it moves up from there. The one exception is a gap through the stop, when the first 30 minutes decide.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate.
questions.simple: False. The size came from the first stop, so moving it down means risking more than you planned.

deeper.trap: There is one exception, and it is not about nerve. If a stock gaps down through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)

questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The gate is a close in the upper half of the range. A close in the top quarter is a grade cue, not a gate. It helps the grade, but a close in the upper half still counts.
questions.lesson_line: Upper half is the gate. Top quarter is a grade cue.
questions.simple: False, because the gap day only has to close in the upper half of its range, and the top quarter is a grade cue.

questions.q: If an EP opens above your 3R level, the rule is to sell a third at the open.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy, and we usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. A 3, 5 or 7 day push, or about 5 to 10R, is often the best place to sell, so a sell at the open can come too early. Selling part into a big gap is an optional judgment, never a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A price past 3R is not a sell signal. The first sell is a judgment.
questions.simple: False. A gap past 3R is not an automatic sell, because the best sells often come later, into a multi-day push.

questions.lesson_line: Short of a full day's volume by 10:00 means no day-one buy.

Take it; holding the gap is enough
Half now and half at the close
Buy the close if it holds the gap

questions.lesson_line: No crowd in the first 30 minutes, no day-one buy.

wrong.Half now and half at the close: Splitting the buy does not fix missing volume. We buy the full size once, at one price.
wrong.Buy the close if it holds the gap: Our day-one buy is an opening-range buy with the volume on pace, not a close buy.

Kullamagi: good news on a neglected stock can start a multi-month move, so part comes off into strength and the rest trails.

questions.simple: True, because EPs can start long moves. Selling part into strength and trailing the rest catches the trend.

Exactly on the day's low so far

Under the base low from months ago
